extracted.intended_audience: comedians and writers crafting short-form jokes for Twitter / social media
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing 1–3 line joke-tweets that stop scrolling, set a clear premise, and deliver a pivoting punch within Twitter's short-form constraints. Emphasizes economy of words, placement of the punch, and industry-minded professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hook (line 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hook in line 1: a sentence that makes scrolling stop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Line 1 must arrest attention immediately — something that makes someone pause their scroll. The Amram checklist asks: 'Does line 1 stop scrolling?' Avoid overly clever hooks that the premise can't follow up on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise (line 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Premise in line 2: the wrong assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The premise should set up a wrong assumption the audience can accept quickly. Make the premise universal enough to 'land outside your bubble' and avoid relying on niche Twitter-only context that only the writer or a tight circle understands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch (line 3 / final clause)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pivot/punch should come in the final clause of the tweet, not the first. Do not put the punch at the start (it may be lost when the tweet is retweeted). The working rubric asks: 'Is the punch in the FINAL clause, not the first?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-line variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Variation: a single line that does all three by structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single well-structured line can simultaneously provide hook, premise, and punch. Consider whether the sentence architecture accomplishes the setup and pivot compactly without additional clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hook–premise alignment / Avoid over-clever hooks
rubrics_metrics.description: The hook is too clever; the premise can't catch up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't lead with an overly clever or oblique hook that the rest of the tweet doesn't support. Ensure the premise follows naturally from the hook and is reachable by most readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid insider/Twitter-only premises
rubrics_metrics.description: The premise requires Twitter context only the writer has.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the joke's setup depends on niche context, inside jokes, or prior-thread knowledge that most readers don't have, it will fail to land. Make premises broad enough to work 'outside your bubble.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch placement anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: The punch is at the start of the tweet (gone by retweet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Putting the punch early loses the surprise on resharing; always structure so the punch is at the end or final clause to survive truncation/retweets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial self-acknowledgment / thanking yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: The author thanked themselves at the end ('lol I'm sorry').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adding self-apologetic or self-congratulatory tags at the end of the joke (e.g., 'lol I'm sorry'), which undermines the punch and reads as insecurity or an attempt to coach the audience's reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word economy / concision
rubrics_metrics.description: 280 chars is too many. Aim for 140.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be ruthless with words. Cut filler words such as 'just,' 'really,' 'very,' 'literally,' 'kind of.' Replace 'I think that...' with plain assertion. Replace participial phrases ('having said that...') with full sentences. The thread's rule: if the joke needs extra words to explain, shorten and sharpen instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific filler-word and hedging cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut 'just,' 'really,' 'very,' 'literally,' 'kind of.' Replace hedges with assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audit for weakeners and hedges; remove them or convert hedged statements into confident assertions. This preserves punch economy and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic tightening (avoid participial hedges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace participial phrases ('having said that...') with sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert dangling or prolonging structures into clear, direct sentences to maintain rhythm and allow the punch to land without buildup that wastes characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reply rule / no self-clarifying replies
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't reply to your own tweet to clarify the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a joke requires a follow-up reply from the author to explain or clarify, it's not finished. Delete and rewrite the original tweet — do not append clarifications or reply to your own tweet to patch comprehension gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry Twitter professional stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: The pros are reading. Treat every tweet as a writing sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider each tweet as a calling card: strong tweets can help you get staffed; poor tweets can cost you opportunities. The working checklist asks: 'Could a TV showrunner read it as a writing sample?' — use that as a professional filter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amram-inflected working rubric (six evaluative questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A concise checklist to evaluate a tweet: 1) Does line 1 stop scrolling? 2) Is the premise universal enough to land outside your bubble? 3) Is the punch in the FINAL clause, not the first? 4) Have you cut every filler word? 5) Did you avoid replying to clarify? 6) Could a TV showrunner read it as a writing sample?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this six-question rubric as a final pass. It synthesizes attention, premise accessibility, punch placement, concision, independence from clarifying replies, and professional presentation.
